topic: TypeScript 5.4 NoInfer: stopping a secondary parameter from widening a generic
text:
Your generic function accepts a value it should reject, and TypeScript is happy about it.

The example from the TypeScript 5.4 release notes:

function createStreetLight<C extends string>(
  colors: C[],
  defaultColor?: C
) {}

createStreetLight(["red", "yellow", "green"], "blue"); // allowed

Both arguments are inference sites, so C widens to include "blue".

The fix is NoInfer<C> (TypeScript 5.4+) on the parameter that shouldn't contribute candidates: defaultColor?: NoInfer<C>

Now "colors" is the only source of truth, and "blue" is a compile error.

Takeaway: when one argument defines the valid set, wrap the others in NoInfer.

Where in your codebase would a generic like this be quietly accepting bad input?

image.alt: Paper cut-out comparison of a TypeScript generic that accepts blue without NoInfer and rejects it with NoInfer, signed Ali Hassan, alihexan.com
